summary: This document updates RFC 5880 by defining a small set of interval values that Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) implementations should support. Some implementations can only use a few timer values, so two peers might fail to find an interval both can run. Having a common set makes sure they can always agree.

eli5.summary: Two friends want to check on each other every few seconds, but each can only use certain timers. This note says everyone should know a few common timers, so any two friends can always pick one that works.

questions: how do bfd peers agree on an interval
subtitle: A small set of BFD timer intervals every implementation should support, so two peers can always agree on one.

tldr.problem: Some BFD implementations, especially hardware-based ones, support only a few interval values. Two such peers may be unable to find an interval both can run.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Common Intervals of 3.3 msec, 10 msec, 20 msec, 50 msec, 100 msec and 1 sec. An implementation should support all of them that are equal to or slower than its own fastest interval, and adjustment always moves toward slower values.
tldr.outcome: Peers are guaranteed to reach a commonly supported interval, and implementations may still support extra values.

facts.label: Common Intervals
facts.value: 3.3 msec, 10 msec, 20 msec, 50 msec, 100 msec, 1 sec

today: RFC 7419 is an Informational RFC that updates RFC 5880. Nothing in the unit metadata says it has been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Intervals Need Agreement
sections.content:
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) peers negotiate a transmission interval and a detection time as described in RFC 5880. That RFC says nothing about what to do when a speaker cannot support the calculated value. Software timers with fine granularity hid the issue, because the error stayed small compared to the 25 percent jitter.

Requests now exist for very fast intervals, down to 3.3 msec for the MPLS Transport Profile, and for large numbers of sessions. Vendors have moved timers and timeout detection to network processors, FPGAs and other hardware, which may offer only a few interval values. That can cause interoperability problems. This RFC updates RFC 5880 with a recommended common set.
sections.eli5: The old way used a flexible stopwatch. New fast machines use clocks with only a few buttons, and sometimes two machines have no button in common.

sections.title: The Problem With Few Supported Intervals
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example. Vendor A supports 10 msec, 100 msec and 1 sec in hardware. Vendor B supports every value from 20 msec with 1 msec granularity. A asks for 10 msec, B uses 20 msec, and the negotiated value is 20 msec, which A cannot run.

Both workarounds have problems. A could advertise the next larger interval, 100 msec, but that jumps far from operator expectations. A could break RFC 5880 by transmitting at 10 msec and using an adjusted multiplier M' = 2 * M on receive, but then B may drop up to 50% of packets if it uses an ingress rate policer expecting 20 msec.

It gets worse if B supports only 50 msec, 500 msec and 2 sec. Even if both walk through all their supported intervals, they never agree.
sections.eli5: One friend can only wait 10 seconds, 100 seconds or 1000 seconds. The other wants 20. Jumping to 100 is a big change, and cheating is not allowed.

sections.title: The Common Interval Set
sections.content:
The requirement is that a BFD implementation should support all Common Interval values that are equal to or larger than the fastest interval it supports. The set is 3.3 msec, 10 msec, 20 msec, 50 msec, 100 msec and 1 sec. In addition, a 10 sec interval and multiplier values up to 255 are recommended to support graceful restart.

Adjustment is always toward larger (slower) values when the peer's proposal is not supported. In the example, A (fastest 10 msec) supports 10, 20, 50, 100 msec and 1 sec, and B (fastest 20 msec) supports 20, 50, 100 msec and 1 sec. Both remain free to support extra values. Supporting an interval means advertising it in DesiredMinTxInterval or RequiredMinRxInterval and providing timers reasonably close to it. No new precision requirements are added.
sections.eli5: Everyone agrees on a short list of shared timer settings. Everyone keeps every shared setting that is slower than their fastest one, so there is always a match.

sections.title: Why These Values and How Peers Converge
sections.content:
Appendix A balances too few values (big jumps) against too many (higher cost). The 3.3 msec value is required by MPLS-TP to support a defect detection time of 10 msec. The 10 msec value reflects general consensus. The 20 msec value avoids a large gap and allows 50-60 msec detection with a multiplier of 2. The 50 msec value is widely deployed. The 100 msec value allows reuse of Y.1731 implementations. The 1 sec value is the one mentioned in RFC 5880. A 10 sec interval with a multiplier of 255 gives a timeout of 42.5 minutes and is kept outside the set because it is for graceful restart.

Appendix B shows that even when two routers support different extra intervals (for example Common Intervals plus 200 msec versus plus 300 msec), they go through several Poll Sequences with the Final bit and end at 1 sec. Reaching a common value is guaranteed.
sections.eli5: Each shared setting has a reason, such as matching an existing device. If two friends have different extra settings, they take turns offering slower ones until they land on one they share.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it introduces no additional security concerns. The security considerations of BFD in RFC 5880 and related documents apply to devices implementing BFD, whether or not the Common Interval set is implemented.
sections.eli5: Agreeing on common timer settings adds no new dangers. The old safety rules still apply.
